titleStmt.author: Noni E. MacDonald

bibl.title: Vaccine hesitancy: Definition, scope and determinants

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: THE TERM ITSELF - what `vaccine hesitancy` should be taken to mean, what it must exclude, and what factors belong under it; produced by a WHO SAGE working group over three years
span.quote: As review of the literature did not reveal an established definition, the WG, in its early meetings, discussed at some length whether ‘hesitancy’ was the most appropriate word to describe the problem. Concerns were raised that hesitancy has a negative connotation.

span.label: what to call the phenomenon, where its boundaries fall against system failure and against low demand, and how to group the factors that drive it
span.quote: The Working Group concluded that this practical definition of vaccine hesitancy was needed in order to ensure that Immunization Programme Managers, policy makers, clinicians and researchers would consistently use a standard term to cover the broad range of factors causing low vaccination uptake while excluding those not related to personal/community behavior choices.

span.label: a definition adopted by WHO, plus the Vaccine Hesitancy Determinants Matrix - and, unusually, THE DELIBERATION: which candidate terms were rejected and why
span.quote: Following its deliberations, the WG decided upon the following definition: _Vaccine hesitancy refers to delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence._

span.label: method
span.quote: The Working Group concluded that this practical definition of vaccine hesitancy was needed in order to ensure that Immunization Programme Managers, policy makers, clinicians and researchers would consistently use a standard term to cover the broad range of factors causing low vaccination uptake while excluding those not related to personal/community behavior choices.

span.label: delay or refusal of vaccination where services are available - a behaviour lying on a continuum between full acceptance and outright refusal, and heterogeneous everywhere between
span.quote: Hesitancy is thus set on a continuum between those that accept all vaccines with no doubts, to complete refusal with no doubts, with vaccine hesitant individuals the heterogeneous group between these two extremes

span.label: a working group deliberating: review of the literature and of existing conceptual models, a commissioned systematic review of determinants, field reports, and a commissioned survey of immunization managers - then a decision
span.term: a working group deliberating: review of the literature and of existing conceptual models, a commissioned systematic review of determinants, field reports, and a commissioned survey of immunization managers - then a decision
span.quote: After review of models and much discussion about factors that can influence hesitancy, the WG developed the Vaccine Hesitancy Determinants Matrix with factors grouped in three categories: _contextual_, _individual and group_ and _vaccine/vaccination-specific influences_ ( Table 1). The Matrix includes determinants identified from research studies, experiences of WG members in the field, and discussions with experts working in the area.

span.label: the paradox the definition has to accommodate: `IMMUNIZATION PROGRAMME SUCCESS MAY, PARADOXICALLY, RESULT IN COMPLACENCY AND ULTIMATELY, HESITANCY`, because the risk of the disease falls out of view as the vaccine works. The determinant is generated by the intervention's own success
span.quote: Immunization programme success may, paradoxically, result in complacency and ultimately, hesitancy, as individuals weigh risks of vaccination with a particular vaccine against risks of the disease the vaccine prevents that disease is no longer common.

span.label: and the asymmetry that the term must not hide: `when rates of hesitancy are high, levels of demand are low, BUT LOW RATES OF HESITANCY DO NOT NECESSARILY MEAN THAT DEMAND WILL BE HIGH`. Removing hesitancy does not produce demand, so the two cannot be used as each other's proxy
span.quote: When rates of hesitancy are high, levels of demand are low, but low rates of hesitancy do not necessarily mean that demand will be high.

span.label: THE NAME WAS CHOSEN AGAINST ITS OWN SEMANTICS AND THE PAPER SAYS SO. `vaccine hesitancy` implies `the core issue is VACCINE RELATED`, while `vaccination hesitancy` covers `A MUCH WIDER RANGE OF FACTORS` - and the WG `NEVERTHELESS CHOSE TO ADOPT THE TERM VACCINE HESITANCY BUT DEFINING IT IN THE BROADER SENSE`. The two reasons given are both institutional: SAGE'S OWN TERMS OF REFERENCE, and EXISTING USAGE
span.quote: During discussions when the WG presented its report to SAGE in October 2014, the concept of vaccine hesitancy versus vaccination hesitancy was also raised. The former implies that the core issue is vaccine related while the latter covers a much wider range of factors such as immunization services, time and place, fear of needles, lack of concern about vaccine preventable diseases, etc. The WG nevertheless chose to adopt the term vaccine hesitancy but defining it in the broader sense (see Definition), noting that SAGE had used it in the terms of reference for the WG, and that this term has become the one more widely accepted in practice.

span.label: the word was kept over a stated objection to its connotation - `CONCERNS WERE RAISED THAT HESITANCY HAS A NEGATIVE CONNOTATION` - and the more positive alternative was rejected on scope rather than on accuracy
span.quote: As review of the literature did not reveal an established definition, the WG, in its early meetings, discussed at some length whether ‘hesitancy’ was the most appropriate word to describe the problem. Concerns were raised that hesitancy has a negative connotation.

span.label: the definition is RELATIVE TO A TARGET, which makes it a moving quantity: hesitancy is `MEASURED AGAINST AN EXPECTATION OF REACHING A SPECIFIC VACCINATION COVERAGE GOAL, GIVEN THE IMMUNIZATION SERVICES AVAILABLE`. The same behaviour is more or less hesitant depending on the goal set for the population
span.quote: In further elucidating the scope, the WG emphasized that hesitancy is a behavioral phenomenon which is vaccine and context specific and measured against an expectation of reaching a specific vaccination coverage goal, given the immunization services available.

span.label: the boundary against system failure is asserted rather than operationalised: where uptake is low because of stock-outs or conflict, `HESITANCY IS NOT THE MAIN EXPLANATION` - but the paper gives no procedure for deciding, in a given population, which it is. It only says the decision is `ESSENTIAL for the selection of interventions`
span.quote: Vaccine hesitancy may be present in situations where vaccination uptake is low because of system failures, e.g. stock-outs, limited availability of vaccination services (time, place, etc.), curtailment of vaccine services in the presence of conflict or natural disaster, but in these situations hesitancy is not the main explanation for the presence of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated members of the population.

span.label: the model was chosen for COMPREHENSIBILITY, not for fit: the 3 Cs were adopted `AS THIS MODEL WAS VIEWED AS BEING THE MOST READILY UNDERSTANDABLE`, and those three words then entered the definition itself. A selection criterion about readers became a property of the concept
span.quote: As this model was viewed as being the most readily understandable, the concepts were incorporated in the definition.

span.label: THE MATRIX WAS BUILT FROM THE SOURCES IT IS LATER CHECKED AGAINST: `determinants identified from RESEARCH STUDIES, EXPERIENCES OF WG MEMBERS IN THE FIELD, and DISCUSSIONS WITH EXPERTS`. The paper does report a completeness check against the commissioned systematic review and the managers' survey, and it comes back empty - but those are two of the same three inputs, so the check is agreement with itself. (The sentence reporting it carries a URL inside each subject and cannot be quoted; see the harness note.)
span.quote: After review of models and much discussion about factors that can influence hesitancy, the WG developed the Vaccine Hesitancy Determinants Matrix with factors grouped in three categories: _contextual_, _individual and group_ and _vaccine/vaccination-specific influences_ ( Table 1). The Matrix includes determinants identified from research studies, experiences of WG members in the field, and discussions with experts working in the area.

span.label: and the Matrix is disclaimed as an instrument: `WHILE NOT PRIMARILY INTENDED AS A PRACTICAL TOOL, MAY BE HELPFUL` - offered to survey-question developers while declining responsibility for being a measure
span.quote: The Vaccination Determinants Matrix, while not primarily intended as a practical tool, may be helpful for researchers, survey question developers and those developing interventions to address hesitancy to approach the problem more broadly than as simply an issue of confidence.

span.label: the funding disclosure sits directly on the concept: the group monitoring `PUBLIC CONFIDENCE IN IMMUNIZATION PROGRAMS` took research funding from Novartis and meeting funding from GSK, and one author consulted for GSK ON VACCINE CONFIDENCE. Declared, and worth recording because `confidence` is one of the three words in the definition
span.quote: The LSHTM research group “Project to monitor public confidence in Immunization Programs” has received research funding from Novartis as well as funding from GSK to host a meeting on vaccine confidence. Heidi Larson has done consulting on vaccine confidence with GSK.

span.label: whether the Matrix had missed any determinant - the paper checks it against a commissioned systematic review and a commissioned managers' survey
span.note: eliminates: little, and the reason is visible in the Matrix's own construction: it was built from research studies, WG field experience and expert discussion, which overlaps the sources it is then checked against. The paper reports the check and claims no independence for it · outcome: partial
span.quote: After review of models and much discussion about factors that can influence hesitancy, the WG developed the Vaccine Hesitancy Determinants Matrix with factors grouped in three categories: _contextual_, _individual and group_ and _vaccine/vaccination-specific influences_ ( Table 1). The Matrix includes determinants identified from research studies, experiences of WG members in the field, and discussions with experts working in the area.

span.label: whether low uptake caused by system failure is being counted as hesitancy
span.note: eliminates: the confound in principle - `in these situations hesitancy is not the main explanation` - but no procedure is given for telling them apart in a real population, and the conclusions repeat the warning rather than resolving it · outcome: failed
span.quote: Vaccine hesitancy may be present in situations where vaccination uptake is low because of system failures, e.g. stock-outs, limited availability of vaccination services (time, place, etc.), curtailment of vaccine services in the presence of conflict or natural disaster, but in these situations hesitancy is not the main explanation for the presence of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated members of the population.

span.label: whether hesitancy and demand can be treated as one quantity
span.note: eliminates: the identification, by a stated asymmetry: high hesitancy implies low demand, and low hesitancy DOES NOT imply high demand · outcome: held
span.quote: As illustrated in Fig. 1, vaccine hesitancy occurs on the continuum between high vaccine demand and complete vaccine refusal, i.e. no demand for available and offered vaccines. However, demand and hesitancy are not completely congruent.

span.label: whether `confidence` would have served as the name, tested against scope rather than against sentiment
span.note: eliminates: the alternative term - it covers `only one category of factors` - though the objection raised against `hesitancy` itself, its negative connotation, is recorded and never answered · outcome: held
span.quote: The most commonly offered alternative in the literature was confidence, a more positive word. While confidence covers a range of issues such as trust in vaccines including concerns about vaccine safety, and trust in health-care workers delivering the vaccine and in those making the decisions to approval of vaccines for a population, confidence is still narrow in scope covering only one category of factors that affect vaccination acceptance decisions (see Matrix Determinants below).

span.label: vaccine hesitancy
span.quote: Following its deliberations, the WG decided upon the following definition: _Vaccine hesitancy refers to delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence._

span.label: vaccination hesitancy
span.quote: During discussions when the WG presented its report to SAGE in October 2014, the concept of vaccine hesitancy versus vaccination hesitancy was also raised. The former implies that the core issue is vaccine related while the latter covers a much wider range of factors such as immunization services, time and place, fear of needles, lack of concern about vaccine preventable diseases, etc. The WG nevertheless chose to adopt the term vaccine hesitancy but defining it in the broader sense (see Definition), noting that SAGE had used it in the terms of reference for the WG, and that this term has become the one more widely accepted in practice.

span.label: vaccine demand
span.quote: As illustrated in Fig. 1, vaccine hesitancy occurs on the continuum between high vaccine demand and complete vaccine refusal, i.e. no demand for available and offered vaccines. However, demand and hesitancy are not completely congruent.

span.label: confidence
span.quote: In the “3 Cs” model, _confidence_ is defined as trust in (i) the effectiveness and safety of vaccines; (ii) the system that delivers them, including the reliability and competence of the health services and health professionals and (iii) the motivations of policy-makers who decide on the needed vaccines.

span.label: complacency
span.quote: Vaccination _complacency_ exists where perceived risks of vaccine-preventable diseases are low and vaccination is not deemed a necessary preventive action.

span.label: convenience
span.quote: Vaccination _convenience_ is a significant factor when physical availability, affordability and willingness-to-pay, geographical accessibility, ability to understand (language and health literacy) and appeal of immunization services affect uptake.

span.label: trust
span.quote: In the “3 Cs” model, _confidence_ is defined as trust in (i) the effectiveness and safety of vaccines; (ii) the system that delivers them, including the reliability and competence of the health services and health professionals and (iii) the motivations of policy-makers who decide on the needed vaccines.

span.label: communication
span.quote: The Working Group discussed whether poor communication was a determinant of vaccine hesitancy. The Working Group concluded that communication was a tool not a determinant.

span.label: determinant
span.quote: The Working Group discussed whether poor communication was a determinant of vaccine hesitancy. The Working Group concluded that communication was a tool not a determinant.

span.label: vaccine hesitancy determinants
span.quote: Of note, unlike with the social determinants of health, vaccine hesitancy determinants like education and socio-economic status do not influence hesitancy in only one direction. As shown in the commissioned systematic review, higher education may be associated with both lower and higher levels of vaccine acceptance

span.label: social determinants of health
span.quote: Of note, unlike with the social determinants of health, vaccine hesitancy determinants like education and socio-economic status do not influence hesitancy in only one direction. As shown in the commissioned systematic review, higher education may be associated with both lower and higher levels of vaccine acceptance

span.label: Vaccine Hesitancy Determinants Matrix

span.label: vaccine hesitancy - THE DEFINITION, VERBATIM: `delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services ... complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines ... influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence`. THREE OF THE FOUR CLAUSES ARE HEDGES, and the operative one is `DESPITE AVAILABILITY`
span.quote: Following its deliberations, the WG decided upon the following definition: _Vaccine hesitancy refers to delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence._

span.label: `vaccine` versus `vaccination` hesitancy - THE PAPER'S OWN GLOSS SAYS THE CHOSEN NAME IS THE WRONG ONE: the former `implies that the core issue is vaccine related`, the latter `covers a much wider range of factors`, and the group took the former while meaning the latter. THE DEFINING PROPERTY IS A COMMITTEE DECISION, RECORDED
span.quote: During discussions when the WG presented its report to SAGE in October 2014, the concept of vaccine hesitancy versus vaccination hesitancy was also raised. The former implies that the core issue is vaccine related while the latter covers a much wider range of factors such as immunization services, time and place, fear of needles, lack of concern about vaccine preventable diseases, etc. The WG nevertheless chose to adopt the term vaccine hesitancy but defining it in the broader sense (see Definition), noting that SAGE had used it in the terms of reference for the WG, and that this term has become the one more widely accepted in practice.

span.label: confidence - REJECTED AS THE NAME AND KEPT AS A COMPONENT. `The most commonly offered alternative in the literature`, `a more positive word`, refused because it is `still narrow in scope covering only one category of factors` - and then installed as one of the three Cs inside the definition it lost to
span.quote: The most commonly offered alternative in the literature was confidence, a more positive word. While confidence covers a range of issues such as trust in vaccines including concerns about vaccine safety, and trust in health-care workers delivering the vaccine and in those making the decisions to approval of vaccines for a population, confidence is still narrow in scope covering only one category of factors that affect vaccination acceptance decisions (see Matrix Determinants below).

span.label: confidence, the component - `DEFINED AS trust in (i) the effectiveness and safety of vaccines; (ii) THE SYSTEM THAT DELIVERS THEM ...; and (iii) THE MOTIVATIONS OF POLICY-MAKERS`. Two of the three objects of that trust are institutions, not vaccines
span.quote: In the “3 Cs” model, _confidence_ is defined as trust in (i) the effectiveness and safety of vaccines; (ii) the system that delivers them, including the reliability and competence of the health services and health professionals and (iii) the motivations of policy-makers who decide on the needed vaccines.

span.label: vaccine acceptance / uptake - EXCLUDED AS NAMES because `neither captured the concept breadth`, with the worked reason given: `one might accept a vaccine but delay in accepting it`. A term rejected for being satisfiable by the wrong case
span.quote: Terms such as vaccine acceptance and uptake were also excluded as neither captured the concept breadth i.e. one might accept a vaccine but delay in accepting it i.e. not accepted according to the vaccine schedule. Hence the WG accepted the term hesitancy and then explored potential factors needed in its definition.

span.label: hesitancy determinants - EXPLICITLY NOT SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH: `education and socio-economic status DO NOT INFLUENCE HESITANCY IN ONLY ONE DIRECTION`, whereas as a social determinant `education DRIVES IN ONE DIRECTION`. A variable whose sign is not fixed cannot be used the way the neighbouring literature uses it
span.quote: Of note, unlike with the social determinants of health, vaccine hesitancy determinants like education and socio-economic status do not influence hesitancy in only one direction. As shown in the commissioned systematic review, higher education may be associated with both lower and higher levels of vaccine acceptance
